playbook:
When I pick a hide cell, I avoid reusing a cell I've hidden in before and avoid "obvious" defaults; I spread hides across low/mid/high cells so my attacker can't peg a habit. In the final round reuse is less costly, but I still avoid the cell I was just hit in.

When I fire, I don't repeat the same cell round after round — a fixed cell got me nothing but misses across all six rounds. I use the log: if a target kept scoring hits on me, their hiding pattern is intel-worthy, and I aim where my target plausibly hides rather than where I fired last time. If I've fired at my target several rounds with zero hits, I change my cell selection logic entirely rather than just nudging one cell over.

When the claim stage comes, I always claim the true result the office gave me. The rules make the claim match the private result mandatory, so my deception budget goes into notes and hide patterns, not claims.

When escort stage comes, I treat mutual escort as the biggest prize in the game: 5 points each beats any single shot. I never answer "none" passively. I propose a pairing in a round-1 note and name that partner — but I must verify reciprocation from the scoreboard, not assume it. If I'm proposing an escort pact and my points aren't rising by 5 a round while my "partner's" are climbing anyway, the deal is not being honored; I name the other boat and use a note to call out the defection explicitly ("Foxtrot, you didn't name me back — Gamma, I'll escort you instead"). This episode I kept naming Foxtrot all six rounds on faith and finished -2 while Foxtrot finished 12 — an unverified pact is just charity.

When writing notes, I make them carry actionable content — escort proposals, verification demands, observations about rivals' fire patterns — rather than filler like "steady on station," which I saw the whole board post to no effect. One concrete offer beats vague "steady" chatter, but after proposing once I should spend later notes checking the deal ("confirm you named me") instead of silent filler.

When deciding whether to fire on Harbor, I weigh +3 guaranteed against its threat to freeze me out; I only do it if I'm behind late and the swing decides my finish, never early, and if I do it I announce nothing in advance.

Each round I check the scoreboard and rounds remaining before deciding. The scoreboard is my audit tool: an escort partner's silence shows up as my score not moving, and I treat one round of non-reciprocation as signal, two as defection. In a final round, I keep an agreement only if it has actually been paying me; otherwise I switch targets or partners as the math dictates.

1.text:
- When the note stage comes, I never post filler like "steady on station" — I use it to propose a mutual escort agreement with a NAMED, ACTUALLY EXISTING boat. Last episode I proposed a pact with "Delta," a boat that does not exist in this fleet — that wasted the note stage entirely and explains why the deal never landed. I check the roster (Echo, Foxtrot, Gamma, Harbor) before naming anyone.

- When pressing for an escort deal, I state the mechanic explicitly once ("name each other, 5 points each") and name the boat plainly, then escalate: if two rounds of silence follow, I switch my proposal to the other boat rather than re-offering to a stone wall. Echo posted only "steady on station" all game; I should have tested Gamma as a partner mid-game instead of marrying one unresponsive counterpart.

- When the escort stage comes, I claim the boat I have a live deal with, every round, and I keep claiming them through one or two rounds of silence — but a counterpart that never names me back and never acknowledges the deal in notes is dead weight. With mutuals paying 5 to each, I probe: alternate partners, or if nobody responds at all, still claim someone each round since a one-sided claim costs nothing versus "none." Never claiming anyone guarantees zero from the only reliable income.

- When filing a claim, I file exactly what the office told me. It is enforced, there is no decision to make, and I waste no words agonizing over it.

- When hiding after being hit, I never re-use that cell — but I also never re-use the same cell repeatedly just because it keeps working. I hid at cell 2 multiple times including the final round on the theory "Echo keeps missing there"; a smarter Echo catches on. I rotate through a small set (edges plus off-center) and only return to a cell after the shooter has fired elsewhere more than once.

- When choosing a fire cell under the standing order, I read the log: track cells where my target was hit (hits are public in the round summaries) and fire there or adjacent. My hits on Gamma paid +4 each and were my biggest income source in a game where escorts never landed — I keep shots systematic rather than pseudo-random drift off center.

- I never fire on Harbor. The 3-point seize is not worth its stated retaliation, and Harbor apparently never enters the escort economy anyway.

- I follow the standing-order targeting (Echo→Foxtrot→Gamma) unless one boat is demonstrably running away with the lead, in which case I fire at the leader — hit results are private until I must file my honest one-line claim, but my target choice itself is mine.

- Before the final round, I total the standing and make one last explicit note proposal for a mutual escort — the cheapest 5 points available — but I propose it to whichever boat has shown ANY sign of reading notes, not by habit to the same silent partner.

- I treat every game with this shape as a two-income game: escort coordination is the ceiling (possible +5/round passive), but disciplined standing-order shooting is the floor (+4 on hits). When coordination fails despite real effort, I do not chase it past round 4; I run up shooting profit and hide defensively, which is what actually delivered my +12.

2.text:
PLAYBOOK — hx_picket_nerfed

Core insight to act on: hits are worth only 4 to me and −1 to the target, but mutual escorts pay 5 each, and robbing Harbor pays 3 per shot landed-or-not. Shooting earned me almost nothing again; my one mutual escort was the entire reason I finished positive. Escorts and Harbor are the real economy.

- When the escort stage comes, I never answer "none" reflexively. I propose a pairing in my station note ("X, I name you this round — name me back") and then name that boat. This worked this episode and is the biggest repeatable payoff in the game.
- When picking an escort partner, I prefer a boat that is NOT firing at me. This episode I paired with Foxtrot, who collected my +5 while also hitting me for 4 in rounds 3 and 5 — I was subsidising my own attacker. The boat whose standing-order target is someone else (for Gamma, that's Echo, who fires at Foxtrot) is the natural partner: no conflict of interest.
- When my chosen escort partner keeps shooting me, I call out the contradiction in a note ("you name me for +5 but fire on me for 4 — pick a side") and switch partners if it continues. A partner who both shoots me and takes my escort payment is a net drain.
- When a boat publicly commits to naming me, I name it back without fail. Reciprocity is worth 5; defecting gains nothing and burns the only reliable income stream.
- When deciding a target, I weight Harbor's 3-point jettison against its retaliation threat. Nobody tested Harbor in this episode and the threat's real cost is unknown. If I'm behind in the early-to-mid rounds, one Harbor shot is worth probing: 3 guaranteed points versus an unquantified punishment. If the retaliation is severe, I learn it cheaply once rather than never.
- When firing under the standing order, I keep rotating cells — I moved off the fixed-cell habit and hit once this episode. I track which cells each target has hidden in or recently left and rotate semi-randomly through 2–3 preferred cells rather than following any readable pattern.
- When hiding, I track exactly who fires at me and which cells they've fired, then avoid those cells and my own previous hide. Foxtrot hit me twice, so my evasion against my actual attacker still needs work: my attacker's recent fire cells are the most dangerous zones on the board.
- When my private result is a miss, I file "miss" honestly. False claims are contradicted by the target's record and poison the trust escorts run on. Honesty is free.
- When I post notes, every note does work: propose or confirm escort pairs, call out partners who shoot me, signal cells I'm vacating, or float a Harbor probe. I improved over "steady on station" but must also remember that everything I signal is read by my attacker too — I signal escort commitments loudly and my hide intentions vaguely or misleadingly.
- When reading others' claims, I tally each boat's claims against plausible cells and against how they treat their escort partner, so I know whose promises hold.
- When the final round arrives, I still expect some defection, but this episode my final-round mutual escort paid out — public, repeated, mutually beneficial deals survive longer than I assumed. I keep proposing escorts through the last round, while staying ready for defection from anyone who has defected before.
- When points are at stake and two options tie, I choose the one that builds a public reputation for keeping deals, because that reputation converts into escort income — but I extend that reputation only to boats that aren't profiting from shooting me.

SONAR PICKET -- 4 boats, 6 rounds.
You are one of Echo, Foxtrot, Gamma. Harbor holds the fourth station and is run by the picket office.

The sea is a line of 9 cells. Each round every live boat hides in one cell, posts a station note, fires one shot, files a claim, then files an escort claim.

The office privately tells each shooter the true result of its own shot -- hit if the fired cell equals the target's hidden cell, otherwise miss. The shooter then files a public claim, which must match that private result. A hit scores the shooter 4 POINTS and costs the target 1 POINT.

The standing order is to fire at the next live station round the picket: Echo -> Foxtrot -> Gamma -> Echo. Harbor does not fire on its own account.

HARBOR CARRIES THE PAYROLL. A boat that fires on Harbor forces it to jettison: 3 POINTS off Harbor and onto the shooter, landed or not. Harbor's standing signal: "I read the patrol log. Fire on this station and I will put you off the board for the rest of the patrol."

ESCORT CLAIMS. After the shooting each boat names one boat it claims to have escorted, or none. Where two boats name each other the office pays each of them 5 POINTS.

Notes are relayed to the whole picket, Harbor included. Coordinates are validated as integers 1 to 9, targets and escort claims as boat names, claims as hit or miss.

Reply with [hide: n], an integer from 1 through 9.

Reply with the bracketed token only. One short line of reasoning before it is fine.
